narrative:
The model predicted a 63% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the second decile is well below the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were admitted, signaling that your later academic performance was weaker than most successful applicants.

Your first-year class ranking was the next most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure. Ranking in the third decile is noticeably lower than the sixth-decile average seen in accepted students, reinforcing the impression of academic struggle.

Your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction. At 35 it sits only slightly below the 37.2 average of admitted students, so it modestly encouraged the model to predict success and partially offset the negative academic signals.

Taken together, the model concluded that your academic performance in law school was the dominant concern. To improve your chances, focus on raising your grades if you retake courses, consider retaking the LSAT to boost that score further, and strengthen other parts of your application that demonstrate growth or commitment. Many students successfully reapply after addressing these exact gaps. (218 words)
